title: Complex candidate and potential blue wave threaten Nevada's safe red House seat
content:
Northern Nevada’s congressional seat has long been a reliably red district, represented by a Republican since the district was drawn in the early 1980s. The seat’s history reflects a consistent pattern of Republican dominance in the region.

This year, however, the race has become competitive. A complicated candidate and a potential blue wave could change that, putting the district’s long‑standing partisan alignment at risk.
summary: Northern Nevada has a reliably red congressional seat represented by a Republican since the early 1980s. A complicated candidate and a potential blue wave this year could change that.

title: Widdecombe suspect accused of trying to break into Farage's home
content:
Joshua Kerry, 28, has been accused of attempting to break into the home of Nigel Farage. The suspect, linked to the Widdecombe incident, appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court to face the charges.

Following his court appearance, Kerry was remanded in custody.
summary: Joshua Kerry, 28, appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court and was remanded in custody.
author: BBC Politics

title: Heatstroke ruined his health. Years before, it took the life of another farm worker at the same company
content:
Farm labor contractor Carlos Vargas Moreno and other workers on H-2A agricultural visas were exposed to hazardous heat conditions while weeding a watermelon field in Goldsboro, North Carolina, on July 19, 2022. The workday began at 7:00 a.m. and continued until 4:00 p.m., during which the temperature reached 90°F (32°C) and the heat index hit 98.3°F. Workers took two 15-minute breaks and ate a one-hour lunch outdoors, conditions that the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (Niosh) heat safety app defines as “hazardous” for outdoor laborers.

The contractor is accused of exposing laborers to heat-related health hazards that ruined the health of one worker and previously took the life of another farm worker at the same company. Despite these incidents, the company continues to bring hundreds of migrant farm workers to North Carolina.
summary: A farm labor contractor exposed laborers on H-2A agricultural visas to heat-related health hazards, but is still bringing hundreds of migrant farm workers to North CarolinaIt was 4pm and 90F (32C) when Carlos Vargas Moreno and other farm workers set out to weed a watermelon field in Goldsboro, North Carolina, on 19 July 2022. The work day had begun at 7am and included two 15-minute breaks and a one-hour lunch eaten outdoors.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Curtin Study Finds Nearly Half of Concussion Patients Still Suffering After One Year
content:
A new study from Curtin University indicates that nearly 50% of individuals who suffer a concussion continue to experience issues one year after the injury. The research also identified specific factors that place patients at the highest risk for developing long-term symptoms.

Mental health conditions and sleep disorders were highlighted as key risk factors contributing to the persistence of these symptoms.
summary: A new Curtin University study found that almost half of people who experience a concussion still have problems a year later. The study also identified factors that put patients at greatest risk for long-term symptoms.

title: Flu Cases Rise in U.S., Early 2026‑27 Season Expected in West
content: Health authorities have warned that the 2026–27 flu season may be beginning early in some western regions of the United States. This alert coincides with a reported increase in the number of people sick with the flu across the country.
summary: Flu illness is rising across the United States. Health authorities warn that the 2026‑27 flu season may start early in some western regions.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Invention and community engagement help children with autism enjoy music
content:
An invention and community engagement are helping children with autism enjoy music, according to a recent report.  

The invention enables a performer to cue an instrument to begin playing onstage with the wave of a hand or press of a button, creating a more interactive concert experience.
summary: An invention and community engagement help children with autism enjoy music. The invention allows a user to cue an instrument to begin playing onstage with a wave of a hand or a press of a button.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Review links adipocyte ferroptosis to inflammation in obesity
content:
A new review examines adipocyte ferroptosis, the breakdown of fat cells due to oxidation from intracellular iron. The review identifies this process as an emerging molecular mechanism that may contribute to adipose tissue dysfunction.

The authors suggest that iron‑induced oxidation of fat cells can trigger chronic inflammation and metabolic complications associated with obesity. The review highlights the role of ferroptosis in the development of obesity‑related health issues.
summary: A new review examines adipocyte ferroptosis, the breakdown of fat cells due to oxidation from intracellular iron. It proposes this mechanism may contribute to adipose tissue dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and metabolic complications associated with obesity.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Heart disease mortality gaps persist across U.S. counties despite overall decline
content:
Heart disease mortality rates in the United States have continued to decline overall, but significant gaps remain. A county‑by‑cause‑by‑population analysis published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology found that disparities based on race, ethnicity and geographic location persist.

The study shows that while national cardiovascular disease mortality has fallen, the variation in death rates is far greater from one county to another than it is from one state to another. This indicates that local factors continue to drive unequal outcomes in heart disease across the country.
summary: A county‑by‑cause analysis in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology found that cardiovascular disease mortality has declined overall in the U.S. However, disparities by race, ethnicity, and place persist, with county‑level mortality varying far more than state‑level.

title: Gene expression linked to survival differs by kidney cancer subtype
content:
Gene expression linked to survival differs by kidney cancer subtype

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common form of kidney cancer, accounting for about 90 % of kidney cancers. It develops when abnormal cells in the kidney's small tubules begin to grow uncontrollably. RCC has several subtypes that differ in their origin, molecular characteristics and genetic makeup.
summary: Renal cell carcinoma accounts for about 90% of kidney cancers and arises from abnormal growth in the kidney's small tubules. The disease has several subtypes that vary in origin, molecular characteristics, and genetic makeup.

title: WHO warns against obesity drugs for children under 10
content:
The World Health Organization has released new global guidelines that caution against the use of obesity drugs for children under the age of ten.  

The guidelines state that care should focus on healthy eating and exercise rather than medicines such as weight‑loss injections.
summary: The World Health Organization says care should focus on healthy eating and exercise. It warns against medicines such as weight‑loss injections for children under 10.
author: BBC Health

title: McDonald's sued for using AI tool to set franchise pricing
content:
McDonald’s is facing a federal lawsuit alleging that it used an artificial‑intelligence tool to set prices across its independently owned franchises.  

The suit claims the AI tool allows those franchises to exchange nonpublic price and sales information, a practice prosecutors say violates antitrust laws and has unfairly inflated menu prices for consumers.  

Most McDonald’s restaurants in the United States are independently owned and are said to set prices individually under company policy. Antitrust laws require businesses to set prices independently from their competitors, as coordinating prices can stifle competition and raise costs for consumers.  

The case is currently pending in federal court.
summary: A federal lawsuit accuses McDonald’s of using an AI tool to set prices for its independently owned U.S. franchises, allegedly violating antitrust laws and inflating menu prices. The suit claims the tool enables franchises to share nonpublic price and sales information, contrary to company policy that requires independent price setting.
author: Guardian Business

title: Trump’s Iowa Steel Plant Project Faces Doubts Over Delivery
content:
Skepticism mires Trump’s Iowa steel plant project: ‘Promises are not the same as jobs’

The Trump administration’s announcement of a $15 billion steel plant in Lee County, Iowa, has raised doubts about whether the project will be built and delivered as promised. Critics point to the president’s record on steel policy as a source of concern.

Trump has long portrayed himself as a “man of steel,” from White House photoshopping him to look like Superman to enacting steel tariffs and approving the sale of US Steel to Japan’s Nippon Steel, which included a “golden” share for the U.S. government. The new plant is to be built by India‑based Mesabi Metallics, but questions remain over the feasibility of the project.

The project’s viability is under scrutiny, with observers questioning whether the promised jobs and production will materialize.
summary: The Trump administration plans to build the largest U.S. steel plant, a $15bn facility in Lee County, Iowa, by India-based Mesabi Metallics. Critics question whether the plant will be built and delivered as promised, citing Trump’s record.
author: Guardian Business

title: Drought cuts wheat harvest in 2026 and raises dairy farmers' costs
content:
Drought conditions have sharply reduced farm output, with wheat harvests in 2026 falling far below previous levels and dairy producers confronting higher operating costs.  

The lower wheat yields and rising expenses for dairy farms illustrate the dual pressure on agricultural producers, highlighting the broader impact of the drought on the sector.
summary: Drought led to a much smaller wheat harvest in 2026. It also caused dairy farmers' expenses to increase.
author: BBC Business

title: Penguin poop fertilizes snow algae blooms, speeding Antarctic melt
content:
A new study indicates that penguin droppings are fertilizing snow algae blooms along the Antarctic Peninsula, resulting in dense green algae patches along the coastline. These nutrient-rich deposits sustain the growth of the algae in the snow.

The expanding areas of green snow melt more rapidly than clean, white snow. This accelerated melting process potentially speeds up the spread of snow- and ice-free areas across Antarctica.
summary: Penguin poop fertilizes snow algae blooms along the Antarctic Peninsula, feeding dense green algae patches along the coastline. These expanding stretches of green snow melt faster than clean, white snow, potentially speeding up the spread of snow‑and ice‑free areas of Antarctica.
author: Phys.org

title: ICC approves trial of pink balls in Tests affected by bad light
content:
The International Cricket Council (ICC) approved a trial of pink balls in Test matches in June this year, targeting games expected to be affected by poor lighting conditions. The use of the pink ball is subject to prior agreement from both participating teams.

This development builds on the introduction of the pink ball for day-night matches more than a decade ago.
summary: The International Cricket Council approved a trial of pink balls in Test matches expected to be affected by bad light. This trial is subject to prior agreement from both teams.
author: Phys.org

title: Techno-optimistic scientists take fewer climate actions, study finds
content:
A recent study indicates that scientists holding techno-optimistic views regarding climate change are less likely to take personal action to address the issue. Specifically, researchers who believe technology will largely solve climate-related problems are 23% less likely to engage in civic climate action than those who disagree with this perspective.

Additionally, the study found that these techno-optimistic scientists are 18% less likely to make high-impact lifestyle changes compared to their counterparts who do not hold this belief.
summary: Scientists who believe technology will largely solve climate change problems are 23% less likely to engage in civic climate action. They are also 18% less likely to make high-impact lifestyle changes compared with scientists who disagree with this belief.
author: Phys.org

title: New framework guides relocation of endangered species outside historical range
content: A new framework aimed at guiding the decision to move endangered species outside their historical ranges to prevent extinction has been published in the journal Conservation Science and Practice. This development marks the conclusion of a multiyear, Pacific-wide initiative. The University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa served as a central supporting participant in this effort.
summary: A new framework to guide the decision to move endangered species outside their historical range was published in Conservation Science and Practice. The multiyear Pacific-wide effort, in which the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa played a central supporting role, produced the framework.
author: Phys.org

title: OpenAI Releases Hundreds of Mathematical Papers Simultaneously
content:
OpenAI announced that it has released 722 mathematical discoveries in a single batch, a move that has surprised the mathematical community.

The announcement follows the company’s simultaneous release of hundreds of papers, underscoring AI’s growing capability in mathematics.

Mathematicians have expressed astonishment at the scale and speed of the new findings.
summary: OpenAI released hundreds of papers at once, showcasing its growing mathematical capabilities. The simultaneous release surprised mathematicians.
author: New Scientist

title: NASA Measures Earth’s Center of Mass Shifts
content:
Earth’s center of mass is constantly on the move, shifting by a few millimeters as enormous amounts of water, ice, and even air migrate around the planet with the seasons.  

NASA scientists have developed a more precise way to track these tiny swings using laser‑range satellites, GPS data, and measurements of how water and ice deform Earth’s crust.
summary: Earth’s center of mass shifts by a few millimeters as water, ice, and air move seasonally. NASA scientists have developed a precise method using laser‑range satellites, GPS data, and measurements of how water and ice deform Earth’s crust.
author: Science Daily

title: Webb finds atmosphere on scorching lava world HD 3167 b
content:
The James Webb Space Telescope has found strong evidence that the rocky lava world HD 3167 b possesses an atmosphere, even though the planet orbits its star every 24 hours under extreme heat.  

The discovery is surprising because HD 3167 b is a hot, rocky planet that was expected to lose its atmosphere.  Scientists say the finding could help them understand how rocky planets retain atmospheres and what the young, molten Earth may once have looked like.
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has found strong evidence that the rocky lava world HD 3167 b has an atmosphere, despite circling its star every 24 hours under extreme heat. The discovery could help scientists understand how rocky planets retain atmospheres and what the young, molten Earth may once have looked like.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists reprogram immune cells inside the body to fight cancer
content:
Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a method to generate cancer‑fighting CAR‑T cells directly inside the body, potentially bypassing the slow and expensive process of removing, engineering, and reinfusing a patient’s immune cells.  

The researchers used a two‑particle delivery system to send CRISPR gene‑editing tools and new cancer‑targeting DNA specifically into T cells. The DNA was inserted at a precise location in the genome, creating the engineered CAR‑T cells in situ.  

This in‑body approach could avoid the current ex‑vivo manufacturing steps required for CAR‑T therapy.
summary: Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a way to create cancer-fighting CAR-T cells directly inside the body, potentially avoiding the slow and extremely expensive process of removing, engineering, and reinfusing a patient’s immune cells. Using a two-particle delivery system, the researchers sent CRISPR gene-editing tools and new cancer-targeting DNA specifically into T cells, where the DNA was inserted at a precise location in the genome.
author: Science Daily

title: Zoo lions show wild behavior after switching to whole carcasses
content:
Scientists at a zoo altered the feeding routine for their lions by providing whole carcasses on a feast‑and‑fast schedule. The change appeared to bring out more natural behavior.  

Under the new regimen, the lions spent nearly three times longer feeding than before. They also engaged in more tearing and manipulating of food and rested more heavily after meals. During the fasting period, their activity increased gradually, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.
summary: Zoo lions fed whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule spent nearly three times longer feeding, tore and manipulated food more, and rested heavily after meals. Their activity then increased gradually during the fasting period, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.
author: Science Daily

title: Sugar intake during antibiotics linked to gut microbiome disruption
content:
Eating more sugar while taking antibiotics was linked to greater disruption of the gut microbiome and increased growth of potentially harmful bacteria.  

Researchers suggest that temporarily cutting back on sweets during and after antibiotic treatment could be a simple way to reduce this damage, though clinical trials are still needed.
summary: Eating more sugar while taking antibiotics was linked to greater disruption of the gut microbiome and increased growth of potentially harmful bacteria. title: James Webb Telescope detects debris indicating Mars‑sized planetary collisions
content:
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope is giving astronomers a glimpse of the violent collisions that may have shaped our own solar system, including the giant impact that created the Moon.  

By studying 21 rare “extreme debris disks” around young stars, researchers found that the dust in these disks can reveal the scale and intensity of planetary collisions.  

The findings show how the dust produced in such collisions can be used to infer the dynamics of planetary impacts.
summary: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope studied 21 extreme debris disks around young stars to observe signs of violent planetary collisions. The dust in these disks suggests impacts involving Mars‑sized worlds, akin to the giant impact thought to have created the Moon.

title: Russian lab worker Darya Shipilova dies after plague centre accident
content:
A 28‑year‑old laboratory worker, Darya Shipilova, died after falling ill at a plague research centre in Siberia. The incident followed a reported accident at the facility, prompting quarantine measures in several hospitals in eastern Russia.

Russia’s health watchdog has stated that Shipilova died of “pneumonia of unknown aetiology.”  Despite this official cause, there is speculation that the worker may have contracted a plague infection.

Lucy Hough spoke to Science Weekly co‑host Madeleine Finlay about the incident.
summary: Quarantine measures have been in place in several hospitals in eastern Russia after 28‑year‑old laboratory worker Darya Shipilova died following a reported accident at a plague research centre in Siberia. title: Karl Deisseroth shares Nobel medicine prize win with family after making school lunches
content:
Stanford University released a video showing Karl Deisseroth informing his two daughters and one son that he has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine. The 54-year-old scientist, who shares the honor with two researchers in Germany, was recognized for his contributions to optogenetics, a field that uses light and genes to control neurons in living brains.

Following the announcement, Deisseroth spent hours on Monday receiving congratulatory calls. Despite the high-profile recognition, he paused to prepare school lunches for his children, who were asleep in the family home in Stanford. This domestic task occurred while he had been speaking with journalists and well-wishers in the middle of the night.
summary: Stanford University shared a video of Karl Deisseroth telling his children he won the Nobel Prize in medicine for his work in optogenetics. The scientist shared the award with two researchers in Germany for research that uses light to control neurons in living brains.

title: Francis Halzen wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for IceCube neutrino work
content:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Francis Halzen.  

Halzen, a Belgian physicist, received the prize for his work on the IceCube detector, which observes ghostly particles called neutrinos. The detector uses sensors buried in the ice to detect these extraterrestrial particles.  

Science editor Ian Sample explained to host Madeleine Finlay how Halzen conceived the idea of using ice‑borne sensors to detect neutrinos.
summary: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Belgian physicist Francis Halzen. He received the prize for his work on the IceCube detector, which observes neutrinos in the ice.

title: Study links post-war sugar rationing to long-term health effects
content:
Research suggests that the first 1,000 days of sugar exposure may leave a lasting mark on health, affecting factors such as blood pressure and aging. This potential long-term impact is being examined in the generation born in Britain during the post-war recovery period, a time when many everyday foods, including sugar, remained subject to strict rationing.

During this era, adults were limited to approximately 3 tablespoons (40g) of sugar per day, while children were restricted to less than a tablespoon. Infants and very young children were expected to consume little to no added sugar. These restrictions were lifted in stages beginning in 1953, with limits on sweets and chocolate removed in February and general sugar rationing ending in September. By the second half of 1954, average sugar consumption in the country had nearly doubled.
summary: Research suggests that sugar exposure during the first 1,000 days of life may leave a decades-long mark on health indicators like blood pressure and aging. British sugar rationing ended in 1953, leading to average consumption almost doubling by late 1954.

title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry Awarded to Kagan and Soai for Mirror-Image Molecule Discovery
content:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Henri B Kagan of Paris-Sud University in France and Kensō Soai of Tokyo University of Science in Japan. The prize recognized their discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, which demonstrated how chemical reactions can produce an overwhelming excess of one of two mirror-image forms of a molecule.

This scientific breakthrough has aided the understanding of how medicines work in the body.
summary: Henri B Kagan of Paris‑Sud University and Kensō Soai of Tokyo University of Science received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Their discovery showed how chemical reactions can produce an overwhelming excess of one of two mirror‑image forms of a molecule, aiding understanding of how medicines work in the body.

content:

Hall was a public intellectual who coined the term Thatcherism and, in 1985, warned of the dangers of “authoritarian populism.” His obituary in The Guardian described him as “among the first to identify key questions of the age” and noted he was a seminal figure in postwar Black British history. He died in 2014 at the age of 82.

content:

The study, which compiled evidence from 100 individuals whose intimate images were shared online without consent, found that many complaints are dismissed or not recognised as criminal offences.  

The findings have prompted the super‑complaint to challenge the handling of such cases, a matter highlighted by former prime minister Keir Starmer, who called image‑based abuse a national emergency.

content:
Israel is preparing for its first national elections since the Hamas attack of Oct. 7, 2023, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his political rivals centering their campaigns on the fallout from that day.  

Three years after what officials described as the worst security failure in Israel’s history, the incident is now seen as a threat to Netanyahu’s career, the country’s longest‑serving prime minister, according to France 24’s Noga Tarnopolsky reporting from Jerusalem.
summary: Israel is preparing for its first elections since the Hamas attack on Oct. 7, 2023. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his opponents are centering the attack in their campaigns, and the security failure now threatens to end his career.
author: France 24

title: Houthis claim strikes on Aden and Riyadh airports amid Yemen fighting
content:
Yemen’s Houthi movement said it carried out strikes on both Aden and Riyadh airports as fighting in the country escalated.  

Aden International Airport was hit in an attack attributed to the Houthis, part of a broader effort by the group to target key transport hubs.  

The intensified conflict between government forces and the Houthis has displaced around 200,000 people.
summary: The Houthis claimed strikes on Aden International Airport and Riyadh airports. Around 200,000 people have been displaced by the fighting between government forces and the Houthis.
author: DW World

title: China’s Golden Week shows cautious consumer spending despite travel surge
content: Chinese visitors are returning home after the 13‑day Golden Week holiday, a period that saw a surge in travel across the country.  Despite the increase in trips, their spending remained subdued, prompting analysts to question the strength of domestic demand in China, the world’s second‑largest economy.
summary: Chinese visitors are returning from trips after the 13‑day Golden Week holiday. Their subdued spending has raised fresh questions about domestic demand in the world’s second‑largest economy.
author: DW World

title: South Sudan's first general election set for Dec 22 amid credibility doubts
content:
South Sudan’s first general election is scheduled for December 22, but its prospects remain uncertain.  

Officials and observers say that ongoing insecurity, heightened political tensions and the fact that voter registration has not yet begun have raised doubts about whether the poll can be conducted credibly.
summary: South Sudan's first general election is scheduled for December 22. Insecurity, political tensions and the failure to begin voter registration have raised doubts about holding a credible poll.
author: DW World

title: Israeli demolition in At Tur, East Jerusalem displaces 69 Palestinians
content:
Israeli authorities approved the demolition of a residential building in the At Tur area of East Jerusalem on Tuesday, displacing sixty‑nine Palestinians, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

More than half of those displaced were children. OCHA reported the demolition and the resulting displacement of the residents.
summary: Sixty‑nine Palestinians, more than half of them children, were displaced on Tuesday after Israeli authorities green‑lit the demolition of their residential building in the At Tur area of East Jerusalem. The UN aid coordination office (OCHA) reported the displacement.
author: UN News

title: Rocket revolution expands access to space launches
content:
The “rocket revolution” is widening the door to space, according to the latest commentary on launch capabilities.  

For many years, only a relatively small group of national space programmes could send payloads beyond Earth, but that situation is now changing.
summary: Launching beyond Earth was once limited to a relatively small number of national space programmes. That is now changing.
author: UN News

title: WHO issues first global child obesity guidelines as rates rise to 8%
content:
The United Nations World Health Organization (WHO) has issued its first global guidelines on child obesity as the condition continues to rise sharply worldwide.  

According to WHO data, obesity among children and adolescents aged five to 19 has quadrupled since 1990, increasing from two percent to roughly eight percent of that age group.
summary: The UN World Health Organization released its first global guidelines on child obesity. Child and adolescent obesity has quadrupled since 1990, rising from two percent to around eight percent among 5‑19 year olds.
author: UN News

title: Governments urge UN reform at New York General Assembly to match modern world
content:
Governments are urging the United Nations to modernize, warning that the organization must reflect today’s world or risk losing trust. The call for reform was a central theme at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month.

During the debate on UN reform, a diverse range of Member States voiced a strikingly common refrain, questioning whether the UN can remain relevant if it continues to look and act as it did when it was founded in 1945. The consensus underscores growing pressure on the UN to adapt its structures and practices to contemporary realities.
summary: The General Assembly in New York held a debate on UN reform last month, drawing a common refrain from a diverse range of Member States. Members questioned whether the UN can stay relevant if it continues to look and act like the organization created in 1945.
author: UN News

title: WHO warns funding gap endangers health response in Yemen
content:
The World Health Organization warned that a critical funding gap is endangering the health response in Yemen. WHO officials said that significantly more resources are needed to scale up its operations in the country.

The warning comes as the conflict in Yemen escalates and health needs continue to rise, prompting the agency to call for urgent additional funding to sustain and expand its response.
summary: The World Health Organization warned that a critical funding gap threatens its health response in Yemen. It said significantly more resources are needed to scale up the response amid escalating conflict and rising needs.
author: UN News

title: Parti Québécois wins Quebec election but falls short of majority, referendum doubtful
content:
The Parti Québécois (PQ) won Monday’s Quebec provincial election, adding 56 seats and more than doubling its vote share from the 2022 contest, giving the party its first taste of power in 14 years.  Despite the surge, the PQ fell five seats short of a majority in the National Assembly.

The shortfall undermines the party’s pledge to hold a sovereignty referendum after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office in 2028, a promise now described as “nearly impossible.”  Analysts note that the result comes amid a bruising trade dispute with the Trump administration, further complicating any push toward separation.
summary: The Parti Québécois won Monday’s Quebec election, adding 56 seats and more than doubling its vote share from 2022, giving it its first taste of power in 14 years. However, the party finished five seats short of a majority, making its pledge to hold a sovereignty referendum after Donald Trump leaves office in 2028 unlikely.
author: Guardian World

title: Flávio Bolsonaro leads first round of Brazil election, alarming climate activists
content:
Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election this week has been described as a grim jolt for climate campaigners. An inquest is under way to understand why President Lula’s success in curbing Amazon deforestation has not translated into electoral support.

Campaigners warn that if Bolsonaro maintains the advantage he established, the Amazon rainforest could face “more fire, more ash, more crime, more death” and be driven further toward a point of no return over the next four years. The concern appears to be greater among the international community than among voters in Latin America’s biggest, richest and most biodiverse nation.
summary: Flávio Bolsonaro established a lead in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election this week. Climate campaigners say his potential four‑year term could increase Amazon fires, ash, crime and deaths, reversing President Lula’s gains in curbing deforestation.
author: Guardian World

title: Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re‑democratise’ Brazil, sparking fears of authoritarian rule
content:
Flávio Bolsonaro secured a surprise first‑round victory, positioning him as the far‑right frontrunner to become Brazil’s next president. His win has been described as a rapid rise for the “House of Bolsonaro,” prompting heightened scrutiny of his political agenda.

In his post‑victory remarks, Bolsonaro pledged to “re‑democratise” Brazil, a statement that critics say could signal a continuation of the authoritarian approach associated with his father, disgraced ex‑president Jair Bolsonaro. Observers warn that such rhetoric may pave the way for a shift toward authoritarian rule if Flávio assumes office.

Brazil’s current democratic framework dates back to the 1980s, when the nation emerged from a 21‑year dictatorship that Jair Bolsonaro has publicly praised. The prospect of a new administration echoing those authoritarian sentiments has intensified concerns about the country’s democratic future.
summary: Flávio Bolsonaro, the far‑right frontrunner, secured a surprise first‑round victory in Brazil’s presidential race. He has vowed to “re‑democratise” Brazil, prompting critics to warn that his win could extend the authoritarian legacy of his father, disgraced ex‑president Jair Bolsonaro.
author: Guardian World

title: Israeli soldier filmed assaulting Palestinian woman during West Bank raid
content:
An Israeli soldier was filmed assaulting a Palestinian woman during a raid on a family home in the occupied West Bank. The incident was captured on video as the soldier entered the residence.

The assault occurred while the soldier was conducting the raid, targeting a family dwelling in the territory. The footage shows the soldier physically attacking the woman during the operation.

The video of the assault has been released, documenting the soldier’s actions against the Palestinian woman during the raid.
summary: An Israeli soldier was filmed assaulting a Palestinian woman. The incident occurred during a raid on a family home in the occupied West Bank.

title: Coco Gauff calls online racist abuse at China Open draining after early exit
content:
Coco Gauff said the online racist abuse she endured during the China Open was “draining.” The U.S. tennis star made the comments after she failed to reach the quarterfinals of the tournament.  

Gauff admitted that the racism she suffered exhausted her following her exit from the event.
summary: Coco Gauff said the online racist abuse she faced during the China Open was draining. The US tennis star was eliminated before reaching the quarterfinals.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai win Nobel chemistry prize for mirror‑image work
content:
Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have been awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their “mirror image” work on asymmetric molecules.  

The prize honors the scientists for solving the mystery of asymmetric molecules, a breakthrough that has aided the manufacture of pharmaceuticals.  

The award underscores the impact of their research on drug production.
summary: Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on mirror‑image molecules. Their research solved the mystery of asymmetric molecules and has helped in the manufacture of pharmaceuticals.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Saudi Arabia defeats UAE 2-0 to claim fourth Arabian Gulf Cup after 22-year gap
content:
Saudi Arabia defeated the United Arab Emirates 2‑0 to capture the Arabian Gulf Cup, ending a 22‑year wait for the title.  

Goals from Hammam Al‑Hammami and Firas al‑Buraikan secured the win and gave the hosts their fourth Arabian Gulf Cup trophy.
summary: Saudi Arabia beat UAE 2-0 in the Arabian Gulf Cup final. Goals from Hammam Al-Hammami and Firas al-Buraikan gave the hosts their fourth Arabian Gulf Cup trophy, ending a 22-year wait.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Okinawa governor urges Japan action after US Marine Devin Jacob Ballard arrested
content:
The governor of Okinawa has called on the Japanese government to take action after U.S. Marine Devin Jacob Ballard was arrested on suspicion of strangling 39‑year‑old Anna Yagi.  

The arrest has sparked growing anger among local residents.  

Ballard’s detention follows the allegation that he killed Yagi, prompting the governor’s appeal for a response from Japanese authorities.
summary: The Okinawa governor urged Japan to act following the arrest of a US Marine. US Marine Devin Jacob Ballard was arrested on suspicion of strangling 39‑year‑old Anna Yagi, prompting growing anger.
author: Al Jazeera

title: South Korea to tighten military exemption rules for Asian Games gold medallists
content: South Korea announced it will consider cutting military exemption benefits for athletes who win gold medals at the Asian Games. The proposal follows a public backlash over comments made by athletes about the Asian Games. Authorities said the move aims to address criticism and reassess the exemption policy for gold‑medal winners.
summary: South Korea says it will cut military exemptions for gold medallists. The decision follows backlash over athletes' Asian Games comments.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Paramount-Warner merger raises press freedom concerns over chairman's ties to Trump, Israel
content:
The proposed merger of Paramount and Warner has ignited concerns that it could threaten press freedom. Critics point to the deal’s potential impact on the media landscape and the independence of news outlets.

The chairman’s family connections to former President Donald Trump and to Israel have prompted questions about editorial independence at CNN and CBS, raising further doubts about how the consolidation might affect journalistic autonomy.
summary: The proposed Paramount-Warner merger has sparked fears about press freedom. The chairman's family ties to Trump and Israel raise questions over editorial independence at CNN and CBS.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Pakistan subsidises petrol for millions, but some in need left out
content:
Pakistan’s government has introduced a petrol subsidy that now benefits millions of citizens. The relief program lowers the cost of fuel for a large segment of the population.

However, some economists warn that the subsidy does not reach the people who need it most, leaving a portion of the population without assistance.
summary: The Pakistani government has subsidised petrol for millions of people. Some economists caution that those most needing help are left out.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Ten linked to Kenya's first Ebola case quarantined amid screening concerns
content:
Ten people linked to Kenya’s first‑ever Ebola case have been placed under quarantine as screening concerns grow.  

The index patient traveled through multiple cities in the Democratic Republic of Congo, drove to Uganda and ultimately flew to Kenya.  

The quarantine of the ten contacts underscores the heightened vigilance of Kenyan health authorities.
summary: Ten people linked to Kenya's first-ever Ebola case have been placed in quarantine as screening concerns grow. The patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, drove to Uganda and eventually flew to Kenya.
author: BBC World

title: Sri Lanka's ex-first lady, 73, arrested over alleged misuse of children's hospital donations
content:
Sri Lanka’s former first lady, a 73‑year‑old woman, was arrested on suspicion of involvement in the misuse of charitable contributions.  

Authorities say the arrest stems from allegations that a charity linked to her misappropriated donations intended for a children’s hospital.
summary: The 73-year-old ex-first lady of Sri Lanka has been arrested. She is accused of being linked to a charity that misused donations intended for a children's hospital.
author: BBC World

title: Trump to speak with Putin about Russian lab worker's death
content:
Former President Donald Trump is set to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin about the death of a laboratory worker in Russia, according to the headline.  

Officials and observers have expressed concerns that the worker’s death may have been caused by pneumonic plague, prompting demands for greater transparency from Russian authorities.  

Calls for more openness from Russia have intensified in response to the plague‑related fears.
summary: Trump will speak with Putin about the death of a lab worker in Russia. Fears that the death may have been caused by pneumonic plague have prompted calls for more transparency from Russia.
author: BBC World

title: Justin Ellis helps US cap a perfect international window with 1-0 win over Canada
content:
Justin Ellis scored the decisive goal in a 1-0 victory over Canada, securing a fourth win in four matches for the United States during a perfect international window. The match, described as chippy and at times ugly, was managed by referee Steven Madrigal, who was noted for paying tribute to the history of the referee’s whistle.

The article highlights the evolution of officiating tools, referencing Joseph Hudson, a Birmingham-bred tool maker who founded Acme Whistles. Hudson introduced his signature product to an FA Cup match in 1878, replacing the prior practice of referees waving a white handkerchief to signal fouls. This innovation occurred nearly 150 years before the recent match between the United States and Canada.
summary: Justin Ellis helped the United States defeat Canada 1-0, capping a perfect international window. The win completed the US's streak of victories.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Lionel Messi bids tearful farewell to Argentina after scoring in 3-0 win over Benin
content:
Lionel Messi concluded his 21-year international career on Tuesday with a tearful farewell to Argentina fans in Buenos Aires. The 39-year-old, widely regarded as the greatest football player in history, made his final appearance for the former world champions in front of 85,000 supporters.

In a decisive match, Messi scored his 126th international goal, helping Argentina secure a 3-0 victory over Benin.
summary: Lionel Messi ended his 21-year international career in a 3-0 victory over Benin, scoring his 126th international goal. The match drew 85,000 fans in Buenos Aires as Messi bid farewell to Argentina.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Wrexham's new Kop stand signals ambition to reach Premier League
content: Wrexham’s new Kop stand serves as a signal of the club’s ambition to continue its ascent from the Championship to the Premier League. The project is designed to match the team’s recent rise, reflecting a broader strategic goal to progress to the top tier of English football.
summary: Wrexham's new Kop stand signals the club's ambition to climb from the Championship to the Premier League. The project reflects the club's rising trajectory.
author: BBC Sport

title: Collins, Jackson clash in first Maine Senate debate
content:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson faced off Tuesday in the first debate of their closely contested Senate race in Maine. Collins, a five-term senator and a rare Republican to win statewide in the blue-leaning state, used the debate stage to highlight instances where she has defied her party.

During the discussion, Collins pointed to her pro-choice position and her vote against President Trump’s signature legislation as examples of times she has bucked her party.
summary: Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson faced off in the first debate of their Senate race in Maine. Collins highlighted her pro-choice position and her vote against President Trump’s signature legislation.
author: The Hill

title: Benson, James spar in Michigan gubernatorial debate: 3 takeaways
content: Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Representative John James faced off in a gubernatorial debate hosted by Nexstar’s WOOD-TV on Tuesday. The candidates discussed issues specific to the state in the final month before voters select the next governor of Michigan.
summary: Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson (D) and Rep. John James (R-Mich.) debated on Tuesday, hosted by Nexstar’s WOOD-TV, less than a month before the gubernatorial election. They discussed issues specific to Michigan.

content:

The hour-long debate was hosted by KWQC and took place at St. Ambrose.
summary: The first televised debate between Republican Zach Lahn and Democrat Rob Sand, who are vying to replace retiring Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) next month, was dominated by accusations of carpetbagging, attacks over family wealth, and barbs over culture war issues. The hour-long debate was hosted by KWQC and held at St. Ambrose.

title: Three Arrested in Raid on Gang Accused of Helping Migrants Pretend to Be Gay for Asylum
content: Three individuals were arrested following a raid on a gang alleged to help migrants pretend to be gay in order to secure asylum. The Home Office immigration enforcement officers carried out the operation, targeting members of the gang. Those targeted by the officers are accused of charging migrants up to £4,500 for fabricated evidence.
summary: Three individuals were arrested after a raid on a gang accused of helping migrants pretend to be gay to obtain asylum. The Home Office immigration enforcement officers claim the gang charged migrants up to £4,500 for fabricated evidence.
author: BBC Politics

title: Nobel winner Halzen says years of October 'misery' finally over
content:
Physicist Francis Halzen says the years of October “misery” are finally over.  

Halzen, who has an impressively long list of academic accolades, has long been a contender for the Nobel Prize.  Each October, as the Nobel announcement rolled around, he found himself unable to secure the award, a failure that left him “miserable,” he admits.  

He now declares that the cycle of disappointment has ended, marking a new chapter in his career.
summary: Physicist Francis Halzen says his repeated failures to win the Nobel Prize each October made him miserable. He has a long list of academic accolades, but the Nobel Prize has eluded him.
author: Phys.org

title: Study estimates oyster reefs could generate $12 trillion annually for planetary health
content:
A recent study estimates that the world’s oyster reefs could contribute up to $12 trillion annually to planetary health if they were better managed.  

The researchers calculated the reefs’ potential gross ecosystem product (GEP)—the ecological counterpart of gross domestic product—finding that the reefs deliver trillions of dollars in ecosystem goods and services each year to various aspects of planetary health, including human well‑being.  

The study notes that oyster reefs are vastly underestimated and underutilized. To unlock their full value, oyster reefs around the world must be restored and protected.
summary: A new study calculated the gross ecosystem product of oyster reefs, estimating trillions of dollars in ecosystem goods and services each year. The study says the reefs' full potential can only be realized if they are restored and protected.
author: Phys.org

title: EU faces fierce lobbying over banning PFAS 'forever chemicals'
content:
The European Union faces mounting pressure to ban “forever chemicals.” The debate is intensifying in Brussels over the toxic substances known as PFAS, with industry groups actively seeking as many exemptions as possible.

The fight over PFAS highlights the tension between regulatory efforts to curb the use of these persistent chemicals and industry interests that wish to maintain flexibility in their production and use.
summary: The European Union is under pressure to ban PFAS, also known as 'forever chemicals'. Industry groups in Brussels are seeking as many exemptions as possible.
author: Phys.org

title: Sleep, appetite, gene‑editing experts vie for Nobel chemistry prize
content:
Sleep, appetite, gene‑editing experts contend for Nobel chemistry prize

Research into molecules that regulate sleep and appetite, as well as methods for editing genes, could be among the contenders for the Nobel Prize in chemistry, to be announced Wednesday, commentators say.
summary: Research into molecules that regulate sleep and appetite or methods for editing genes could be among the contenders for the Nobel Prize in chemistry. The prize will be announced Wednesday, commentators say.
author: Phys.org

title: A new way to fight gum disease without wiping out good bacteria
content:
Scientists have discovered that interfering with the chemical signals bacteria use to communicate can shift dental plaque toward a healthier microbial balance.  

The technique, which targets bacterial communication, may enable treatments for gum disease that suppress harmful bacteria while preserving beneficial species.  

Researchers suggest this approach could form the basis for new therapies that control gum‑related infections without wiping out good bacteria.
summary: Scientists discovered that disrupting the chemical messages bacteria use to communicate can push dental plaque toward a healthier microbial balance. The approach could lead to new treatments for gum disease that control harmful bacteria without destroying beneficial species.
author: Science Daily

title: Study of 100 primate species shows humans not hardwired for violence
content:
A recent comparative study of 100 primate species, including humans, challenges the idea that everyday aggression and lethal violence are part of a single behavioral spectrum.  

The research found that species that frequently fight or show mild aggression are not necessarily more likely to kill rivals. Instead, extreme acts such as infanticide and lethal attacks appear to follow their own distinct evolutionary patterns.  

These findings suggest that humans may not be as hardwired for violence as previously thought.
summary: A study comparing 100 primate species, including humans, found that everyday aggression and lethal violence did not evolve as part of the same simple behavioral spectrum. Species that frequently fight or show mild aggression are not necessarily more likely to kill rivals, while extreme acts such as infanticide and lethal attacks appear to follow their own evolutionary patterns.
author: Science Daily

title: LSE study finds techno‑optimist scientists 23% less likely to sign climate petitions
content:
A study from the London School of Economics found that scientists who believe technology will largely solve the problems caused by the climate crisis are less likely to take climate action.

The report shows that these techno‑optimists are 23 % less likely to sign petitions or participate in protests than peers who doubt that technology is the answer. They are also 18 % less likely to adopt high‑impact lifestyle changes, such as reducing flights or switching to a vegan or vegetarian diet.

The findings suggest a link between technology optimism and lower engagement in climate action.
summary: Scientists who believe technology will largely solve climate problems are less likely to engage in civic climate action, a London School of Economics report found. The report says they are 23% less likely to sign petitions or join protests and 18% less likely to make high‑impact lifestyle changes such as reducing flights or adopting a vegan or vegetarian diet.

content:

title: Christa Pike awake a week after lethal injection, still shackled in hospital
content:
Christa Pike is awake a week after a lethal injection attempt, but she remains shackled to a hospital bed with burned and blistered arms, according to reports.

The incident has coincided with Tennessee’s suspension of executions and the resignation of the state’s prison chief.
summary: Christa Pike is awake a week after a lethal injection and remains shackled to a hospital bed with burned and blistered arms. Tennessee has suspended executions and its prison chief has resigned.
